questiontext.text: A neural network's forward computation is represented as which kind of graph?

feedback.text: Correct — operations form a DAG with no cycles.
No — data flows in one direction and there are no cycles.
No — only actual data dependencies create edges.
No — a general DAG can branch and merge, unlike a list.

generalfeedback.text: The forward computation is a directed acyclic graph: nodes are operations, edges are tensors/values.

questiontext.text: In a compute graph, what do the nodes and edges represent?

answer.text: Nodes are operations; edges are the tensors/values flowing between them

feedback.text: Yes — each node computes an op on its incoming values.

answer.text: Nodes are tensors; edges are neurons

feedback.text: No — nodes are operations, not the data itself.

answer.text: Nodes are layers; edges are learning rates

feedback.text: No — edges carry values, not hyperparameters.

generalfeedback.text: Nodes = operations, edges = tensors/values, matching how a DAG models data dependencies.

questiontext.text: In what order must the forward pass evaluate the nodes?

answer.text: Topological order, so every input is ready before a node runs

feedback.text: Correct — a topological order respects all dependencies.
No — a node cannot run before its inputs are computed.
No — names have nothing to do with dependencies.

generalfeedback.text: The forward pass evaluates nodes in topological order so each node's inputs are available.

questiontext.text: How does backpropagation traverse the compute graph?

answer.text: In reverse topological order, accumulating gradients via the chain rule

feedback.text: Yes — reverse-mode autodiff walks the graph backward.

answer.text: In the same forward order as the forward pass

feedback.text: No — gradients flow from outputs back toward inputs.

answer.text: By re-running the forward pass twice

feedback.text: No — one reverse traversal suffices to get all gradients.

generalfeedback.text: Backprop reverses the graph and accumulates gradients (reverse-mode autodiff via the chain rule).

questiontext.text: Which statements about a forward compute graph are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is acyclic, so a valid topological ordering exists

feedback.text: Yes — a DAG always has a topological order.

answer.text: Backpropagation traverses it in reverse to accumulate gradients

feedback.text: Yes — reverse-mode autodiff walks the graph backward.

answer.text: It must contain a cycle to allow gradient flow

feedback.text: No — the forward graph is acyclic; gradients flow along reversed edges.

answer.text: Nodes may be evaluated in any order during the forward pass

feedback.text: No — evaluation must respect topological order.

generalfeedback.text: A forward compute graph is an acyclic DAG evaluated topologically forward and traversed in reverse for gradients.

questiontext.text: A forward compute graph contains no directed cycles.

feedback.text: Correct — it is a directed acyclic graph.
The forward computation is acyclic by construction.

questiontext.text: Backpropagation evaluates the nodes in the same order as the forward pass.

feedback.text: No — backprop traverses the graph in reverse.
Correct — gradients are accumulated in reverse topological order.

questiontext.text: A forward compute graph is a directed acyclic graph, abbreviated ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Accepted — nodes are evaluated in topological order.
Accepted.
